claims.claim: Dover has multiple component-level bridges into AI infrastructure: CPC liquid-cooling connectors and SWEP heat exchangers address the rising thermal load created by dense compute, while capacity investment is expanding physical throughput for larger heat-transfer products.

The structural advantage is diversified participation across cooling components rather than ownership of the whole data-center stack; the counterfactual is that alternative cooling architectures or vertically integrated OEM designs reduce the value captured by standalone connectors/heat exchangers.

causalEdges.mechanism: heat removal requires efficient fluid transfer and heat exchange
lower-pressure-drop fluid connections and heat transfer

risks.risk: Dover captures only component-level economics and can face design substitution, OEM insourcing or pricing pressure.

unknowns.unknown: Exact AI/data-center revenue and backlog contribution remains undisclosed at the Dover consolidated level.

claims.claim: Dover's consolidated 7% Q2 revenue growth and 5% organic growth do not isolate AI cooling; treating the entire company growth rate as data-center exposure would inflate the thesis.

The company itself identifies acquisition integration, customer capital spending, competition/pricing, supply-chain/labor, input inflation and new-product execution as material risks; these are relevant because Dover's AI exposure is embedded inside a diversified acquisition-active industrial portfolio.

risks.risk: AI-cooling contribution can be overstated because Dover does not separately disclose its revenue/margin contribution in the retrieved reporting.
Acquisition mix can obscure organic economics and creates integration/valuation risk.

unknowns.unknown: Customer concentration and share position for Dover's liquid-cooling products remain unquantified in current evidence.
